newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain labour talks progress slowly but no deal yet.
newsitem.headline: Spain labour talks progress slowly but no deal yet.

text.p: Spain's employers and unions failed to strike a deal on crucial labour reforms on Tuesday but said they were making progress and would resume talks on Wednesday.
In a last ditch attempt to clinch a deal before the government moves in and forces an agreement, unions and employers talked intensively for much of the day and late into the night.
There was a flash of hope for a final accord after Tuesday's talks when employers said the negotiations were advancing, albeit slowly, and both sides were moving closer to a deal.
"The efforts that both sides are making to come closer to an accord are impressive and there have been advances," spokesman for employers' association CEOE, Juan Jimenez Aguilar, told reporters.
Unions were also optimistic for an agreement on Wednesday.
"Negotiations are continuing and both sides are trying their hardest to reach a reasonable and balanced agreement," the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) union spokesman Fernando Puig told reporters.

Struggling to suppress Europe's highest unemployment rate, the government is keen to secure an agreement aimed at liberalising its highly rigid labour market and preparing the economy for European Monetary Union (EMU).
It has given unions and employers until early March to reach a deal before it steps in and imposes a package of measures.
But as unions have pointed out, the government knows an accord needs to be voluntary to be truly effective.
Unions warned on Monday that government-imposed reforms would fail and lead to labour disputes.
Previous attempts to impose reforms have had little success and liberalisation measures enforced in 1994 by the previous Socialist administration sparked a 24-hour strike.
The main hurdle in current negotiations lies in a disagreement over dismissal costs.
Employers complain Spain's severance pay is by far the highest in the European Union and dissuades them from hiring staff.
They are demanding an expansion of current dismissal regulations that would effectively cut costs to employers.
At present, labour regulations stipulate that fair worker dismissal can only be justified by economic, technical, organisational or productive reasons.
The majority of contested redundancy cases rule in favour of the sacked employee at a higher cost to businesses.
Redundancies deemed as justifiable by the courts require employers to pay compensation of 20 days per year worked, while unfair dismissal demands payment of 45 days per year.
Employers are demanding the creation of another category that falls between these two which would oblige employers to pay 25 days for each year worked.
In the event that no deal is reached, analysts are sceptical the government will be as radical in its reforms as it is threatening to be.
But if they are not tough enough, analysts fear the government could face a worse scenario after joining EMU with unemployment climbing even higher than the current rate of more than 20 percent.
If, as the government hopes, Spain makes the first wave of EMU in 1999, it will no longer have the recourse of devaluing the peseta to help boost the economy and create jobs, analysts said.
